title: Functions: what they are and why we use them

visuals.title: What happens when a function is called

stages.name: 1. main reaches the call
stages.detail: The statement add(a, b) is met. main pauses at exactly this spot and remembers where to come back.

stages.name: 2. Arguments are copied
stages.detail: The value of each argument is copied into the matching parameter. x gets the value of a, y gets the value of b.

stages.name: 3. The function body runs
stages.detail: The statements between { and } run one by one. The function has its own variables, hidden from main.

stages.name: 4. return sends the answer back
stages.detail: return ends the function. Its value travels back to the place of the call. A void function sends nothing.

stages.name: 5. main continues
stages.detail: The call is replaced by the returned value, and main carries on with the very next step.

visuals.title: Match each part of a function with its meaning

pairs.meaning: The kind of value the function sends back. void means nothing.
The word you write to call the function.
The boxes that receive the values given by the caller.
The first line: return type, name and parameter list.
The statements that do the work.
The statement that makes the function run.

goal: After this you can explain what a function is and why it is useful, name the parts of a function (header, body, call), write a simple function above main(), and follow how control jumps into a function and comes back.
warmup: Think of a busy canteen. The manager does not cook, wash plates and take payment himself. He calls the cook for food, the cashier for payment and the helper for cleaning. Each worker does one job and can be called again and again. In a C++ program, main() is the manager and each function is a worker. A big program becomes a team of small, easy jobs.
definition: A function is a named block of code that does one specific job. It runs only when you call it. Dividing a big program into small functions is called modular programming (a module is one small part). A function has a header (return type, name, parameter list) and a body (the statements inside { }). Why use functions? 1) Reusability: write once, call many times. 2) Readability: main() becomes short and easy to read. 3) Easier testing and debugging: test each worker alone. 4) Teamwork: different people can write different functions. 5) No copy-paste: no repeated code in many places.
howItWorks: Press Play on the pipeline and watch a call. main is running. It meets a call such as add(a, b) and PAUSES. The values of the arguments are copied into the function's parameters. The function body runs from the top. When it reaches return, the function ends and the answer goes back to the place of the call. main then continues with the next step. Look at the trace's call stack: it is a pile of 'who is waiting for whom'. main sits at the bottom. When main calls a function, that function is placed on top. When the function ends, it is removed and main is on top again. In this lesson the functions are written ABOVE main(), so the compiler has already met them when main calls them. (Writing them below main needs a prototype, which comes next week.)

worked.problem: Write a function sayHello() that prints a greeting, and call it from main() between two other messages.
pseudocode: sayHello prints: Hello from a function!
sayHello finishes, control returns to main
worked.flowchartMermaid:
flowchart TD
  A([Start]) --> B[/Print Start/]
  B --> C[Call sayHello]
  C --> D[/Print Hello from a function!/]
  D --> E[Return to main]
  E --> F[/Print End/]
  F --> G([End])

sample.title: A function with no parameters and no return value
sample.expectedOutput:
Start
Hello from a function!
End

explanation.text: The function header. void means it sends nothing back. sayHello is the name. The empty () means it needs no input.
The function body. This line runs only when somebody calls sayHello.
Every program starts at main(). It is the manager.
Runs first. The function has NOT run yet, even though it is written above main.
The function call. main pauses here, sayHello runs, then main continues on the next line.
Runs after the function has finished.

steps.note: The program starts at main(). Functions written above main do not run by themselves.
main prints Start.
main reaches the call sayHello(). main PAUSES and control jumps into the function.
Inside the function body. It prints its message.
The function is finished, so it leaves the stack. main continues from the line AFTER the call and prints End.
main returns 0 and the program ends.

worked.problem: Write a function add(x, y) that returns the sum of two numbers. Call it with variables and with fixed numbers, and print the answers.
pseudocode: s = add(a, b)   (x = 7, y = 5 inside add)
worked.flowchartMermaid:
flowchart TD
  A([Start]) --> B[a = 7, b = 5]
  B --> C["s = add(a, b)"]
  C --> D["x = 7, y = 5 copied"]
  D --> E["return x + y = 12"]
  E --> F[/Print Sum = 12/]
  F --> G["call add(100, 250) returns 350"]
  G --> H[/Print Another sum = 350/]
  H --> I([End])

sample.title: add(): a function that returns a value

explanation.text: Header: return type int, name add, parameter list (int x, int y). The function receives two whole numbers and sends one whole number back.
Calculates x + y and sends the answer back to the place that called add.
Two ordinary variables of main. x and y of add are different boxes.
The call. The values of a and b (7 and 5) are copied into x and y. The returned 12 is stored in s.
Prints the value stored in s.
A call can sit inside another statement. The call is replaced by its return value, 350, before cout prints it.

steps.note: Program starts in main().
main creates a and b.
main calls add(a, b). It pauses. The values 7 and 5 are COPIED into x and y.
x + y = 12. return sends 12 back and ends add.
Back in main, the call is replaced by 12 and stored in s. x and y are gone.
main prints s.
A second call, add(100, 250). Now x is 100 and y is 250.
350 is sent back.
The call became 350, and cout prints it.
main ends the program.

worked.problem: Write a program with a function larger(a, b) that returns the larger of two integers. main must read two integers and print the larger one. Input: 17 42.
pseudocode: IF a > b THEN RETURN a
worked.flowchartMermaid:
flowchart TD
  A([Start]) --> B[/Read p and q/]
  B --> C["Call larger(p, q)"]
  C --> D{a > b?}
  D -->|Yes| E[return a]
  D -->|No| F[return b]
  E --> G[/Print Larger/]
  F --> G
  G --> H([End])

sample.title: Larger of two numbers using a function

explanation.text: Header: returns an int, called larger, takes two ints.
Compare the two numbers that were copied in.
If a is bigger, send a back. The function ends here.
Reached only if a was NOT bigger. Then b is the larger (or equal) one.
main reads two numbers. Reading is done in main, calculating is done in larger: each function does one job.
The call. The returned value is printed by cout.

steps.note: main creates p and q.
cin reads 17 and 42.
main calls larger(p, q). 17 and 42 are copied into a and b.
Is 17 > 42? No. Skip the return a.
return b sends 42 back and ends the function.
The call is replaced by 42 and printed.

variations.when: A fixed job that needs no input and gives no answer
variations.example: void printLine() { cout << "------" << endl; }   // call: printLine();

variations.when: You need an answer from the function
variations.example: int add(int x, int y) { return x + y; }

variations.when: You only want the job done (the returned value, if any, is ignored)
You want to use the returned value straight away
You only want to print the answer

variations.way: Call the same function many times
variations.when: The same job is needed again (the whole point of a function)

mistakes.error: 'sayHello' was not declared in this scope
a function-definition is not allowed here before '{' token
No compiler error (at most a warning that the statement has no effect). Without the brackets () the function is never called, so nothing is printed.

examTips: Learn the parts by heart: header = return type + name + parameter list; body = the statements in { }; call = name(arguments);.
A function does NOT run when it is defined. It runs only when it is called.
Program execution always starts at main(), even if other functions are written above it.
Tracing: when main calls a function, main waits. After the function ends, main continues from the line after the call.
Advantages list for exams: reusability, readability, easier debugging, teamwork, less repetition.
romanSummary: Function code ka ek naam wala block hai jo ek specific kaam karta hai aur sirf tab chalta hai jab usay call kiya jaye.
Faide: code dobara use hota hai, main() chhota aur saaf hota hai, debugging asaan hoti hai.
Function ke parts: header (return type, naam, parameter list), body { } aur call.
Call par main ruk jata hai, function chalta hai, return ke baad main agli line se aage chalta hai.
Is hafte functions main() se upar likhte hain taake compiler unhe pehle dekh le.

quiz.prompt: Which statement is TRUE about a function?
options: It runs only when it is called
It can be called only once
It must be written below main()
quiz.answer: It runs only when it is called
quiz.explanation: A function is a block of code waiting to be called. It can be called many times.

quiz.prompt: Which is NOT an advantage of functions?
options: Each part can be tested separately
quiz.hint: Think about why programmers write functions.
quiz.explanation: Functions give reuse, readability and easier debugging. They do not promise more speed.

quiz.prompt: Where does the program start running?
options: At the first function written in the file
At the function with the shortest name
At the last line of the file

quiz.prompt: After a called function ends, where does main continue?
options: From the line after the call
From the first line of main
quiz.answer: From the line after the call
quiz.explanation: Control returns to the point where the function was called, and the program carries on.

quiz.prompt: Which part of a function holds the statements that do the work?
quiz.hint: It is inside the curly brackets.
quiz.explanation: The body is the set of statements inside { }. The header only describes the function.
